newsitem.title: UK: Study explains why some memories were so vivid.
newsitem.headline: Study explains why some memories were so vivid.

text.p: Emotional experiences could help cement memories into the brain and this might explain why some recollections are so vivid, said a report published on Wednesday.

As well as explaining why many adults remember where they were when U.S. President John Kennedy was shot in 1963, the findings could also help scientists find treatments for memory loss caused by disease and old age, experts said.
Memories are saved on different levels, with some staying in the brain for only a few seconds, others retrievable with some effort, while others are almost permanent.

Scientists know "rehearsal" of information helps strengthen the connections between neurons, or brain cells. It is the pattern of connections between neurons that forms the physical basis of memories.
Proteins are required to make the connections -- and thus memories -- stick, but scientists were unsure whether the brain actually aimed the proteins at each individual recollection.

Uwe Frey at Germany's Federal Institute for Neurobiology in Magdeburg and Richard Morris of the University of Edinburgh experimented on rat brains and found that intense stimulation caused a "wave" of proteins to wash over the brain.
Reporting in the science journal Nature, they said this indicated the process was indiscriminate.
If an animal was feeling intense emotions during a significant experience, memories that would ordinarily be dropped were cemented in with the central recollection.

"Our findings could provide a mechanistic explanation of why inconsequential events are typically remembered for much longer if they occur around the same time as well-remembered events," they wrote in a report in the science journal Nature.
"The vividness of flashbulb' memories may derive, in part, from this cellular mechanism."

Mark Bear, a neuroscientist at the Howard Hughes Institute at Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, said this could explain why many people know just where they were and what they were doing on November 22, 1963, when Kennedy was shot.
They could also "open new avenues for the treatment of memory loss that often accompanies traumatic brain injury, stroke, Alzheimer's disease and normal ageing," he wrote.
Bear compared the process to chalk on a wet blackboard. When the brain is processing an experience, the connections between neurons are like a splatter of water on the blackboard.

Most of the droplets will evaporate and disappear, just like memories of most day-to-day experiences. But if chalk dust gets sprinkled onto the wet spot, it will dry onto the board, leaving a mark where the water was.
The chalk dust is comparable to the protein, Bear said in a telephone interview.
"If you take two erasers and pound them together, you get this big cloud of dust and this dust settles on any wet spot. That is what Frey and Morris suggest happens," he said.
Now the race will be on to find out what causes the protein to appear, Bear said, suggesting it could be a neurotransmitter -- or brain chemical -- like dopamine.
If just one chemical was involved, it could make memory loss much easier to treat, he added, saying the process probably evolved as a survival mechanism.
"If you were being chased by a sabre-toothed tiger it would make sense to remember every detail of your escape route."
